claim: GFP:ATG8CL labelled autophagosomes frequently accumulated around the haustoria in 73% of observations (N = 60).
source: GFP:ATG8CL labelled autophagosomes frequently accumulated around the haustoria (73% of observations, N = 60) labelled by the EHM marker REM1.3 (Figure 1A)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data showing frequency of perihaustorial accumulation, supported by Figure 1A showing confocal microscopy images

claim: In uninfected cells, ATG8CL labelled randomly distributed puncta and the central vacuole.
source: whereas in uninfected cells ATG8CL labelled randomly distributed puncta and the central vacuole (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: Microscopy observations documented in supplementary figure

claim: Perihaustorial ATG8CL-autophagosomes with varying size and shape remain tightly associated with the EHM.
source: Time-lapse microscopy imaging of haustoriated cells in which the tonoplast and EHM are slightly parted away from each other revealed that perihaustorial ATG8CL-autophagosomes with varying size and shape remain tightly associated with the EHM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C and Video 1)
evidence: Time-lapse microscopy data showing spatial association between autophagosomes and EHM

claim: Autophagy deficient GFP:ATG8CLΔ mutant failed to accumulate around the haustoria.
source: Unlike GFP:ATG8CL, autophagy deficient GFP:ATG8CLΔ mutant failed to accumulate around the haustoria (Figure 1B)
evidence: Microscopy data comparing wild-type and mutant constructs

claim: GFP:ATG8CLΔ appeared randomly distributed as puncta that occurred around haustoria in only 14% of the observations (N = 51).
source: GFP:ATG8CLΔ appeared randomly distributed as puncta that occurred around haustoria in only 14% of the observations (N = 51) and did not associate with the EHM (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data showing frequency of perihaustorial localization

claim: The GFP control construct showed only diffuse cytoplasmic signal and did not label any perihaustorial puncta (0% N = 20).
source: The GFP control construct showed only diffuse cytoplasmic signal and did not label any perihaustorial puncta (0% N = 20) (Figure 1C)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data from negative control

claim: GFP:ATG8IL appeared in only 28% of the imaged haustoria (N = 65), typically with no more than a few puncta.
source: Unlike frequently observed GFP:ATG8CL puncta (73% of observations, N = 60) that is abundantly present around the haustoria (Figure 1A), GFP:ATG8IL appeared in only 28% the imaged haustoria (N = 65), typically with no more than a few puncta (Figure 1D)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data comparing ATG8CL and ATG8IL localization

claim: During pathogen infection, ATG8CL-autophagosomes are selectively directed toward the pathogen interface.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that during pathogen infection ATG8CL-autophagosomes are selectively directed toward the pathogen interface.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple microscopy experiments showing differential localization patterns

claim: Silencing of ATG4 resulted in 31.6% ± 6.2 of haustoria associated with GFP:ATG8CL puncta.
source: We observed a notable reduction in frequency of perihaustorial ATG8CL-autophagosomes when ATG4 (31.6% ± 6.2) or ATG9 (39.3 ± 5.2%) is silenced compared to negative control (GUS gene silencing, 63 ± 1.5%) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Quantitative data from RNAi knockdown experiments

claim: Silencing of ATG9 resulted in 39.3% ± 5.2% of haustoria associated with GFP:ATG8CL puncta.
source: We observed a notable reduction in frequency of perihaustorial ATG8CL-autophagosomes when ATG4 (31.6% ± 6.2) or ATG9 (39.3 ± 5.2%) is silenced compared to negative control (GUS gene silencing, 63 ± 1.5%) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Quantitative data from RNAi knockdown experiments

claim: GUS gene silencing (negative control) resulted in 63% ± 1.5% of haustoria associated with GFP:ATG8CL puncta.
source: We observed a notable reduction in frequency of perihaustorial ATG8CL-autophagosomes when ATG4 (31.6% ± 6.2) or ATG9 (39.3 ± 5.2%) is silenced compared to negative control (GUS gene silencing, 63 ± 1.5%) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Quantitative data from control RNAi experiments

claim: The core autophagy machinery is required for perihaustorial accumulation of ATG8CL labelled autophagosomes.
source: These results indicate that the core autophagy machinery is required for perihaustorial accumulation of ATG8CL labelled autophagosomes.
evidence: Conclusion based on RNAi knockdown experiments showing reduced perihaustorial accumulation

claim: Joka2 is a modular protein with multiple domains including an N-terminal Phox and Bem1 (PB1) domain, central zinc finger (ZZ) and NBR1 domains followed by two C-terminal ubiquitin-associated domains (UBA) that flank an AIM.
source: Joka2 is a modular protein with multiple domains including an N-terminal Phox and Bem1 (PB1) domain, central zinc finger (ZZ) and NBR1 domains followed by two C-terminal ubiquitin-associated domains (UBA) that flank an AIM (Zientara-Rytter and Sirko, 2014)
evidence: Protein domain architecture supported by citation to previous literature

claim: PB1 and ZZ domains are implicated in self-oligomerisation and protein-protein interactions.
source: PB1 and ZZ domains are implicated in self-oligomerisation and protein-protein interactions, whereas UBA domains and the AIM bridge Joka2 to the autophagic machinery and the ubiquitinated cargo (Figure 3A)
evidence: Functional annotation of protein domains based on established knowledge

claim: UBA domains and the AIM bridge Joka2 to the autophagic machinery and the ubiquitinated cargo.
source: PB1 and ZZ domains are implicated in self-oligomerisation and protein-protein interactions, whereas UBA domains and the AIM bridge Joka2 to the autophagic machinery and the ubiquitinated cargo (Figure 3A)
evidence: Functional annotation of protein domains based on established knowledge

claim: Autophagosomes labelled by the full length Joka2 fused to BFP accumulated around the haustoria at high frequency (92%, N = 50).
source: Autophagosomes labelled by the full length Joka2 fused to BFP (Joka2:BFP) accumulated around the haustoria at high frequency (92%, N = 50) and localised to the EHM, unlike the BFP vector control (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data showing frequency of perihaustorial localization

claim: Joka2AIM:BFP mutant labelled perihaustorial puncta at lower frequency (74%, N = 42) compared to Joka2:BFP.
source: Intriguingly, Joka2AIM:BFP mutant also labelled perihaustorial puncta, although at lower frequency (74%, N = 42) compared to Joka2:BFP (Figure 3C)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data comparing wild-type and mutant constructs

claim: Joka2Δ1-487 failed to accumulate at the pathogen interface (1%, N = 72).
source: Furthermore, a Joka2 truncate lacking the PB1 and ZZ domains, but retaining the ubiquitin binding and ATG8 interacting motifs (Joka2Δ1-487) showed distribution similar to the BFP vector control and failed to accumulate at the pathogen interface (1%, N = 72) (Figure 3D,E)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data from truncation mutant experiments

claim: Reduced perihaustorial accumulation of Joka2Δ1-487 was not due to reduced protein stability as Joka2:BFPΔ1-487 accumulated at similar protein levels compared to Joka2:BFP.
source: This was not due to reduced protein stability as Joka2:BFPΔ1-487 accumulated at similar protein levels compared to Joka2:BFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Western blot data showing protein expression levels

claim: Joka2-ATG8 interaction is not sufficient for Joka2's recruitment to the perihaustorial puncta.
source: These findings suggest that Joka2-ATG8 interaction is not sufficient for Joka2's recruitment to the perihaustorial puncta and Joka2's oligomerisation and/or association with other proteins mediated by PB1 and ZZ domains are critical for its haustorial accumulation.
evidence: Inference from mutant analysis showing that AIM mutant still localizes but truncation mutant does not

claim: Joka2's oligomerisation and/or association with other proteins mediated by PB1 and ZZ domains are critical for its haustorial accumulation.
source: These findings suggest that Joka2-ATG8 interaction is not sufficient for Joka2's recruitment to the perihaustorial puncta and Joka2's oligomerisation and/or association with other proteins mediated by PB1 and ZZ domains are critical for its haustorial accumulation.
evidence: Inference from domain deletion experiments showing loss of perihaustorial localization

claim: Joka2:BFP fluorescent signal fully overlapped with GFP:ATG8CL labelled perihaustorial autophagosomes (100%, N = 140).
source: Joka2:BFP fluorescent signal fully overlapped with GFP:ATG8CL labelled perihaustorial autophagosomes (100%, N = 140) unlike the BFP:EV (0%, N = 20) indicating Joka2 localizes to perihaustorial ATG8CL autophagosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C)
evidence: Quantitative colocalization data from confocal microscopy

claim: Joka2:BFP also labelled puncta that did not show any GFP:ATG8CL fluorescence suggesting that Joka2 also labels compartments that are not ATG8CL-autophagosomes.
source: Surprisingly, Joka2:BFP also labelled puncta that did not show any GFP:ATG8CL fluorescence suggesting that Joka2 also labels compartments that are not ATG8CL-autophagosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: Microscopy observations showing non-overlapping fluorescent signals

claim: Joka2AIM:BFP produced fluorescence signal at discrete puncta that rarely coincided with perihaustorial ATG8CL-autophagosomes (19%, N = 37).
source: Consistent with this, Joka2AIM:BFP produced fluorescence signal at discrete puncta that rarely coincided with perihaustorial ATG8CL-autophagosomes (19%, N = 37) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Quantitative colocalization data from mutant analysis

claim: Like mammalian autophagy cargo receptors, Joka2 forms oligomers.
source: Like mammalian autophagy cargo receptors, Joka2 forms oligomers (Zientara-Rytter and Sirko, 2014), and this most likely accounts for recruitment of Joka2AIM:BFP to ATG8CL-autophagosomes.
evidence: Protein property supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Joka2 oligomerization most likely accounts for recruitment of Joka2AIM:BFP to ATG8CL-autophagosomes.
source: Like mammalian autophagy cargo receptors, Joka2 forms oligomers (Zientara-Rytter and Sirko, 2014), and this most likely accounts for recruitment of Joka2AIM:BFP to ATG8CL-autophagosomes.
evidence: Mechanistic inference based on oligomerization property and observed localization of AIM mutant

claim: Similar to ATG8CL, Joka2 protein levels were higher in infected leaves compared to the mock infected leaves.
source: We observed that, similar to ATG8CL, Joka2 protein levels were higher in infected leaves compared to the mock infected leaves (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Western blot data comparing protein levels in infected vs. mock-infected samples

claim: ATG8CL/Joka2 mediated antimicrobial autophagy is targeted to the haustorial interface.
source: These results further illustrate that ATG8CL/Joka2 mediated antimicrobial autophagy is targeted to the haustorial interface.
evidence: Conclusion based on protein accumulation data and localization studies

claim: Overexpression of Joka2 restricts pathogen colonisation.
source: Previously we have shown that overexpression of Joka2 restricts pathogen colonisation (Dagdas et al., 2016)
evidence: Reference to previous publication by the authors

claim: Leaves expressing Joka2Δ1-487 conferred only mild resistance compared to full length Joka2.
source: In contrast to leaf patches expressing the full length Joka2, which can accumulate at the perihaustorial autophagosomes (Figure 3B), leaves expressing Joka2Δ1-487 conferred only mild resistance (Figure 3F–G)
evidence: Infection assay data comparing lesion sizes between full-length and truncated constructs

claim: Diversion of plant antimicrobial autophagy towards pathogen interface is critical to limit P. infestans infection.
source: Considered together with the cell biological analyses of Joka2 in haustoriated cells, infection assays suggest that diversion of plant antimicrobial autophagy towards pathogen interface is critical to limit P. infestans infection.
evidence: Conclusion integrating localization data and functional infection assays

claim: The pathogen needs to subvert the biogenesis of antimicrobial Joka2/ATG8CL compartments and/or neutralize their defense related function at the host-pathogen interface.
source: Thus, the pathogen needs to subvert the biogenesis of antimicrobial Joka2/ATG8CL compartments and/or neutralize their defense related function at the host-pathogen interface.
evidence: Inference based on the importance of perihaustorial autophagy for defense

claim: In haustoriated cells, GFP:PexRD54 frequently labelled perihaustorial puncta (70%, N = 36).
source: In haustoriated cells, GFP:PexRD54 frequently labelled perihaustorial puncta (70%, N = 36) (Figure 4A)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data showing frequency of perihaustorial localization

claim: GFP:PexRD54AIM2 rarely detected any puncta around the haustoria (4%, N = 71).
source: However, similar to the GFP control (0%, N = 22), we rarely detected any puncta around the haustoria labelled by GFP:PexRD54AIM2 (4%, N = 71, Figure 4B–C)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data from mutant analysis

claim: ATG8CL binding is critical for recruitment of PexRD54 to the perihaustorial autophagosomes.
source: This suggests that ATG8CL binding is critical for recruitment of PexRD54 to the perihaustorial autophagosomes.
evidence: Inference from comparison of wild-type and AIM mutant localization patterns

claim: BFP:PexRD54 fully overlapped with GFP:ATG8CL across the EHM (100%, N = 73).
source: We observed a full overlap between the two punctate fluorescent signals across the EHM, in contrast to BFP:PexRD54AIM2 and BFP:EV negative controls (100%, N = 73 for PexRD54, 14%, N = 35 for PexRD54AIM2 and 0%, N = 29 for EV control) (Figure 4D–G)

claim: BFP:PexRD54AIM2 showed 14% (N = 35) overlap with GFP:ATG8CL.
source: We observed a full overlap between the two punctate fluorescent signals across the EHM, in contrast to BFP:PexRD54AIM2 and BFP:EV negative controls (100%, N = 73 for PexRD54, 14%, N = 35 for PexRD54AIM2 and 0%, N = 29 for EV control) (Figure 4D–G)
evidence: Quantitative colocalization data from mutant analysis

claim: Detection of perihaustorial PexRD54AIM2 labelled autophagosomes suggests that this mutant can still weakly associate with ATG8CL in vivo or forms higher order molecular complexes with the host autophagy machinery.
source: Although hardly observed (5/35, 14%), detection of perihaustorial PexRD54AIM2 labelled autophagosomes suggests that this mutant can still weakly associate with ATG8CL in vivo or forms higher order molecular complexes with the host autophagy machinery.
evidence: Inference from low-frequency colocalization of AIM mutant with ATG8CL

claim: The ATG8CL selective autophagy pathway that is targeted by P. infestans is diverted to the haustorial interface.
source: Altogether, these findings demonstrate that the ATG8CL selective autophagy pathway that is targeted by P. infestans is diverted to the haustorial interface.
evidence: Conclusion integrating localization data for both host and pathogen proteins

claim: ATG9 is the only transmembrane domain containing ATG protein.
source: A recent study has shown that the plant ATG9 homolog, the only transmembrane domain containing ATG protein, localises to autophagosome biogenesis sites and remains in mobile puncta adjacent to mature autophagosomes (Zhuang et al., 2017)

claim: The plant ATG9 homolog localises to autophagosome biogenesis sites and remains in mobile puncta adjacent to mature autophagosomes.
source: A recent study has shown that the plant ATG9 homolog, the only transmembrane domain containing ATG protein, localises to autophagosome biogenesis sites and remains in mobile puncta adjacent to mature autophagosomes (Zhuang et al., 2017)
evidence: Subcellular localization pattern supported by citation to recent literature

claim: ATG9 is ubiquitously found at the perihaustorial puncta (in >92% of imaged haustoria) neighbouring ATG8CL and Joka2 labelled perihaustorial autophagosomes with a partial yet clear overlap.
source: Transient expression of ATG9:GFP in haustoriated cells revealed that ATG9 is ubiquitously found at the perihaustorial puncta (in >92% of imaged haustoria) neighbouring ATG8CL and Joka2 labelled perihaustorial autophagosomes with a partial yet clear overlap (Figure 5A–C)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data showing frequency and spatial relationship of ATG9 with autophagosomes

claim: In addition to accommodating mature ATG8CL autophagosomes, perihaustorial compartments are hotspots for autophagosome biogenesis.
source: This finding suggests that in addition to accommodating mature ATG8CL autophagosomes, perihaustorial compartments are hotspots for autophagosome biogenesis.
evidence: Inference from ATG9 localization data, as ATG9 marks biogenesis sites

claim: There was a substantial increase in the frequency of haustoria that associate with ATG8CL autophagosomes in infected plant cells overexpressing ATG9:GFP (90%, N = 120) compared to cells expressing GFP as a control (67%, N = 105).
source: Besides, we noted a substantial increase in the frequency of haustoria that associate with ATG8CL autophagosomes in infected plant cells overexpressing ATG9:GFP (90%, N = 120) compared to cells expressing GFP as a control (67%, N = 105) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Quantitative microscopy data comparing overexpression and control conditions

claim: Increasing ATG9 protein levels led to a significant drop in P. infestans infection (p=0.0035, six biological replicates).
source: Strikingly, we repeatedly observed that increasing ATG9 protein levels led to a significant drop in P. infestans infection (p=0.0035, six biological replicates)
evidence: Statistical analysis of infection assay data with p-value and replicate number

claim: Selective autophagy functions as a focal immune response against P. infestans.
source: Overall these results suggest selective autophagy functions as a focal immune response against P. infestans. (Figure 5D–E)
evidence: Conclusion integrating localization and functional infection data

claim: Autophagosomes labelled by the core autophagy protein ATG8CL and the plant autophagy cargo receptor Joka2 are diverted to the EHM.
source: We show that autophagosomes labelled by the core autophagy protein ATG8CL and the plant autophagy cargo receptor Joka2 are diverted to the EHM, and accumulation of Joka2 at this interface is critical for its antimicrobial activity (Figures 1–3)

claim: Accumulation of Joka2 at the EHM is critical for its antimicrobial activity.
source: We show that autophagosomes labelled by the core autophagy protein ATG8CL and the plant autophagy cargo receptor Joka2 are diverted to the EHM, and accumulation of Joka2 at this interface is critical for its antimicrobial activity (Figures 1–3)
evidence: Conclusion from experiments showing that truncation mutant lacking perihaustorial localization has reduced antimicrobial activity

claim: P. infestans RXLR effector PexRD54 accumulated across the EHM.
source: Moreover, P. infestans RXLR effector PexRD54, which functions as a competitive inhibitor of Joka2, also accumulated across the EHM (Figure 4)

claim: PexRD54 functions as a competitive inhibitor of Joka2.
source: Moreover, P. infestans RXLR effector PexRD54, which functions as a competitive inhibitor of Joka2, also accumulated across the EHM (Figure 4)
evidence: Functional characterization likely from previous work by the authors

claim: Previously discovered antagonistic interaction between PexRD54 and Joka2 principally takes place across the EHM, where PexRD54 depletes Joka2 from ATG8CL-autophagosomes to undermine antimicrobial autophagy.
source: These findings suggest that previously discovered antagonistic interaction between PexRD54 and Joka2 principally takes place across the EHM, where PexRD54 depletes Joka2 from ATG8CL-autophagosomes to undermine antimicrobial autophagy.

claim: A similar antagonistic interaction has recently been reported in plasmodium infected hepatocytes, in which a plasmodium virulence factor counteracts functioning of the mammalian xenophagy receptor p62 on the parasitophorous vacuole membrane that accommodates the intracellular plasmodium.
source: A similar antagonistic interaction has recently been reported in plasmodium infected hepatocytes, in which a plasmodium virulence factor counteracts functioning of the mammalian xenophagy receptor p62 on the parasitophorous vacuole membrane that accommodates the intracellular plasmodium (Real et al., 2018)
evidence: Parallel example from animal pathogen system supported by citation

claim: These findings highlight convergent evolution of autophagy related host defenses, guided by autophagy cargo receptors, targeted towards the invading plant and animal pathogens.
source: These findings highlight convergent evolution of autophagy related host defenses, guided by autophagy cargo receptors, targeted towards the invading plant and animal pathogens.
evidence: Evolutionary interpretation based on parallel mechanisms in plant and animal systems

claim: Adapted plant pathogens deploy effector proteins to remodel processes taking place at the perimicrobial host membranes and antagonize the focal immune responses deployed by the host to destroy the invaders.
source: Furthermore, our results illustrate that adapted plant pathogens deploy effector proteins to remodel processes taking place at the perimicrobial host membranes and antagonize the focal immune responses deployed by the host to destroy the invaders.

claim: Recruitment of ATG9 labelled vesicles to perihaustorial region suggests the pathogen interface serves a scaffold for autophagosome formation and defense related autophagy responses.
source: Recruitment of ATG9 labelled vesicles to perihaustorial region suggests the pathogen interface serves a scaffold for autophagosome formation and defense related autophagy responses (Figure 5)

claim: Local autophagosome biogenesis at the pathogen interface would not only eliminate the unnecessary energy spent to transport these defense-related spherical bodies towards the EHM, but more importantly, minimize the time required for their effective deployment at this interface.
source: This would not only eliminate the unnecessary energy spent to transport these defense-related spherical bodies towards the EHM, but more importantly, minimize the time required for their effective deployment at this interface.

claim: Local autophagosome biogenesis at the pathogen interface is reminiscent of the antibacterial autophagy responses mounted by mammalian cells against Salmonella Typhimurium.
source: This is reminiscent of the antibacterial autophagy responses mounted by mammalian cells against Salmonella Typhimurium (Randow et al., 2013)
evidence: Comparison to analogous system in mammalian cells supported by citation

claim: ATG8 gene family has expanded and diversified to different degrees in plant lineages.
source: Surprisingly, ATG8 gene family has expanded and diversified to different degrees in plant lineages (Kellner et al., 2017)
evidence: Evolutionary pattern supported by citation to phylogenetic analysis

claim: The expansion of plant ATG8s appears to have occurred early in evolution, and each plant family carries a unique set of ATG8 isoforms that have diversified over millions of years.
source: The expansion of plant ATG8s appears to have occurred early in evolution, and each plant family carries a unique set of ATG8 isoforms that have diversified over millions of years (Kellner et al., 2017)

claim: It is possible that in different plant families different ATG8 isoforms are specialized to carry out defense-related tasks.
source: Thus, it is possible that in different plant families different ATG8 isoforms are specialized to carry out defense-related tasks.
evidence: Speculation based on observed functional specialization and evolutionary diversification

claim: A phylogenetic analysis of solanaceous plants revealed family-specific groups of ATG8 members that form four distinct clades.
source: A phylogenetic analysis of solanaceous plants revealed family-specific groups of ATG8 members that form four distinct clades (Kellner et al., 2017)
evidence: Phylogenetic classification supported by citation

claim: Unlike ATG8CL, ATG8IL does not accumulate at the haustorial interface during P. infestans infection.
source: Unlike ATG8CL, another solanaceous ATG8 clade member, ATG8IL, does not accumulate at the haustorial interface during P. infestans infection.

claim: Not all autophagic trafficking components are diverted to the haustorial interface.
source: Thus, not all autophagic trafficking components are diverted to the haustorial interface.

claim: Autophagosomes labelled by ATG8IL do not respond to pathogen infection and remain cytosolic.
source: Autophagosomes labelled by ATG8IL do not respond to pathogen infection and remain cytosolic, further highlighting the specialization of ATG8 isoforms in plants that was proposed by Kellner et al (Kellner et al., 2017). (Figure 1)

claim: The differential behavior of ATG8IL further highlights the specialization of ATG8 isoforms in plants that was proposed by Kellner et al.
source: Autophagosomes labelled by ATG8IL do not respond to pathogen infection and remain cytosolic, further highlighting the specialization of ATG8 isoforms in plants that was proposed by Kellner et al (Kellner et al., 2017). (Figure 1)

claim: These findings reveal a novel trafficking route from the cytoplasm to the pathogen interface.
source: These findings reveal a novel trafficking route from the cytoplasm to the pathogen interface and expands our understanding of the biogenesis of the EHM (Bozkurt et al., 2015, 2014; Lu et al., 2012)

claim: The emerging view is that the EHM is formed by the redirection of different endomembrane trafficking pathways, notably the late endocytic pathway and ATG8CL-mediated selective autophagy.
source: The emerging view is that the EHM is formed by the redirection of different endomembrane trafficking pathways, notably the late endocytic pathway and ATG8CL-mediated selective autophagy.

claim: PexRD54-ATG8CL autophagosomes could carry a distinct cargo that substitutes the defense related cargo to redirect molecules towards the pathogen.
source: We hypothesize that the PexRD54-ATG8CL autophagosomes carry a distinct cargo that substitutes the defense related cargo to redirect molecules towards the pathogen.

claim: Pathogen modified double-layered autophagosomes could fuse with the EHM discharging single layered vesicles into the extrahaustorial matrix.
source: Such pathogen modified double-layered autophagosomes could fuse with the EHM discharging single layered vesicles into the extrahaustorial matrix.

claim: Fusion of autophagosomes with the EHM could provide a membrane source for EHM biogenesis.
source: Fusion of autophagosomes with the EHM could provide a membrane source for EHM biogenesis and may account for the extracellular vesicles (EVs) that have been recently reported in several host-microbe interfaces (Deeks and Sánchez-Rodríguez, 2016; Rutter and Innes, 2017)

claim: Fusion of autophagosomes with the EHM may account for the extracellular vesicles (EVs) that have been recently reported in several host-microbe interfaces.
source: Fusion of autophagosomes with the EHM could provide a membrane source for EHM biogenesis and may account for the extracellular vesicles (EVs) that have been recently reported in several host-microbe interfaces (Deeks and Sánchez-Rodríguez, 2016; Rutter and Innes, 2017)

claim: PexRD54 may orchestrate the recruitment of host cargo for delivery as EVs to the host-pathogen interface.
source: Thus, PexRD54 may orchestrate the recruitment of host cargo for delivery as EVs to the host-pathogen interface.

claim: P. infestans produces haustoria, hyphal extensions that invaginate the host cell membrane.

claim: The host accommodation membrane, also known as the extrahaustorial membrane (EHM) sharply contrasts with the adjacent plasma membrane in both protein and lipid composition.

claim: The EHM is not uniform, and multiple membrane sources probably contribute to its biogenesis.
source: Thus, the EHM is not uniform, and multiple membrane sources probably contribute to its biogenesis (Bozkurt et al., 2015)

claim: Multiple trafficking pathways are diverted to haustoria with some degree of specificity.
source: The emerging model is that multiple trafficking pathways are diverted to haustoria with some degree of specificity.

source: In contrast, selective-autophagy employs specialized autophagy cargo receptors that bind ATG8 on autophagosome membranes, and recruit specific cargoes to autophagosomes (Lamb et al., 2013)

source: For instance, to destroy viral particles and restrict viral infection, the plant autophagy cargo receptor Joka2/NBR1 activates antimicrobial autophagy, also known as xenophagy (Hafrén et al., 2017)

claim: The molecular basis of Joka2/NBR1 mediated defense-related autophagy remains unknown.

claim: PexRD54 attenuates defense-related autophagy by depleting Joka2 from autophagosomes.
source: PexRD54 carries an ATG8 interacting motif (AIM) and attenuates defense-related autophagy by depleting Joka2 from autophagosomes (Dagdas et al., 2016)
